About: Motion in a Potential — Bound, Free, or Balanced on the Edge

Source

Lecture
Classical mechanics — energy methods: 1-D motion in a potential landscape V(x)
Simulation
"Motion in a Potential — Bound, Free, or Balanced on the Edge" — energy-diagram mode with a ✓/⚠ counterfactual pair of speed rules
Concept
The height of the total-energy line E relative to the barrier top Vb — not the local slope — decides the fate of the motion: bound oscillation (E < Vb), escape (E > Vb), or the separatrix (E = Vb), where the time to reach the unstable maximum diverges.
Serves
Reading energy diagrams: allowed region, turning points where V(x)=E, KE = E − V(x); classifying equilibria via V″ (stable minimum at x = +1 m, unstable maximum at x = −1 m, barrier Vb = ⅔·s = 0.6667 J at s = 1); critical slowing on the separatrix.
Inquiry
Where along the track is the ball fastest? What changes as E crosses Vb? With E = Vb exactly, does the ball ever arrive at the top?
Misconception
"The ball's speed at a point is set by how steep the potential is there." Slope sets ACCELERATION a = −V′(x)/m; SPEED is set by E − V(x) — fastest at the minimum, zero at turning points.

Motion in a Potential
✦Ask Euler

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet the energy diagram

Let’s get to know the diagram. The curve is V(x) = s(x³/3 − x). The cyan dashed line is the total energy E, and the amber dashes mark the barrier top Vb at x = −1 m. With E below Vb, the ball is trapped in the right-hand valley — released from rest at x₀ ≈ 1.8 m.

2 · Predict — where is it fastest?

Here’s your first prediction. Once the ball is released in this bound well, where along the track do you think it moves fastest?

3 · Watch the energy budget

Let’s watch the energy budget at work. Press ▶ Play if needed. The trail dots space out widest at the bottom, and v → 0 at the turning points where V(x) = E. Now compare the cyan v-arrow with the magenta a-arrow: at x = +1 m, a = 0 while v peaks.

4 · Predict — raising E past Vb

Now let’s give the ball more energy. The amber line is the barrier height. If you raise E above Vb, what do you think happens to the ball?

5 · Escape, then the separatrix

E is now above Vb, so watch the one-pass escape. Then, for something stranger, try Snap E = Vb (separatrix): the ball creeps toward x = −1 m but never arrives — the gap halves every t½ = 0.49 s — forever. That critical energy has a name: the separatrix.

6 · Predict — the two flat points

One last puzzle. Remember, slope sets the acceleration, a = −V′(x)/m. Two points here have zero slope: the valley floor at x = +1 m and the barrier top at x = −1 m.

A ball rests at each one, then gets a tiny nudge. How do you think the two respond?

The landscape and its equilibria
Equilibria where V′ = 0: x = ±1 m. V″(+1 m) = +2s > 0 → stable minimum, V(+1) = −⅔s. V″(−1 m) = −2s < 0 → unstable maximum, barrier Vb = V(−1) = ⅔s (= 0.6667 J at s = 1).
Speed from energy — not from slope
v is set by the gap E − V(x): maximal at the minimum, zero at turning points where V(x) = E. The slope only sets the acceleration a(x) = −V′(x)/m.
The separatrix: time to the top diverges
Linearized near the top (ξ = x + 1) at E = Vb: exponential approach with rate λ = √(2s/m); each halving of the gap costs t½ = ln2/λ. The ball approaches forever — it never arrives.
The ⚠ counterfactual rule (for contrast)
The tested (wrong) rule: speed ∝ steepness, calibration τ = 1 s. It predicts stalling at BOTH x = ±1 m and no dependence on E — contradicted by the observed maximum speed at x = +1 m.

The Physics

Motion in a potential · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim rolls a ball along a potential-energy curve V(x) and draws its fixed total energy E as a line on the same diagram. Reading that one diagram tells you where the ball can go, how fast it moves there, and whether it stays or escapes.

What you'll learn

  • How to read the ball's speed off an energy diagram.
  • What the slope of V(x) does to the ball, and what it does not do.
  • How the total energy decides whether the ball stays or escapes.
  • What happens exactly on the dividing line, and how the curve's two flat points differ.
The curve V(x) = s(x³/3 − x), the energy line E, and the barrier height Vb at the crest.

What's on screen

  • Grey curve: the potential energy V(x) at each position.
  • Dashed cyan line E: the total energy (drag its ⇕ handle).
  • Dashed amber line: the barrier height Vb, at the crest x = −1 m.
  • Ball and trail: dots dropped at equal time steps. White dots: v = 0.
  • Green KE bar, cyan v-arrow and magenta a-arrow on the ball.
  • Chips, top left: type of motion, speed v, and a stopwatch t near the barrier.
See itRun the inquiry's opening scene. Watch for: the ball turning back each time it reaches the dashed energy line.

03

Speed comes from the energy gap

With no friction, E = ½mv² + V(x) stays the same everywhere. So the kinetic energy at any x is the vertical gap from the curve up to the E line:

m = 1 kg in the sim.
  • Bigger gap, faster ball. The gap is largest where V is lowest, at the valley floor x = +1 m.
  • Turning points. The ball can only be where V(x) ≤ E. Where the curve meets the line, KE = 0 and the ball turns round.
E s

These sliders move the sim too.

See itRelease the ball from rest at E = 0.30 J. Watch for: v rising to 1.39 m/s as the ball crosses the valley floor, and falling to 0 at each turning point.
04

The slope sets the acceleration, not the speed

The force on the ball is −V′(x), so the slope of the curve gives the acceleration:

  • At the valley floor the slope is zero, so a = 0, at the very point where v is largest.
  • At a turning point v = 0, but the slope is not zero. The force is still there, so the ball turns back instead of stopping.
  • On the steep stretches the speed changes fastest. Steep means a large acceleration, not a large speed.
See itThe same run, now watching the two arrows. Watch for: the magenta a-arrow shrinking to nothing at the valley floor, just as the cyan v-arrow is longest.
05

Above the barrier, the ball escapes

The crest at x = −1 m is the highest point between the valley and the open slope to the left. Its height is the barrier, Vb = V(−1) = ⅔s (0.667 J at s = 1).

  • E below Vb: bound. The line meets the curve on both sides, so there are two turning points. With no friction, the ball swings between them forever.
  • E above Vb: free. The left turning point is gone. The ball crosses the crest still moving, at √(2(E − Vb)/m), and runs off to the left for good.
  • The starting point is always in the valley, so E alone decides which of the two happens. The steepness of the curve plays no part.
See itRaise E to 0.833 J, above the barrier. Watch for: the ball slowing over the crest without stopping, then leaving to the left as the top-left chip turns to ESCAPED.
06

At exactly the barrier, the ball never arrives

Set E = Vb. The ball reaches the crest with zero speed, and close to it the speed is proportional to the distance ξ = x + 1 still to go:

λ = √(2s/m). The gap shrinks exponentially.
  • The remaining gap halves every t½ = ln 2 · √(m/2s): 0.49 s at s = 1.
  • Every halving costs the same time, so the ball gets ever closer but never reaches x = −1 m. The stopwatch keeps counting.
  • This energy is the separatrix, the boundary between bound and free motion. Just below it, each swing slows near the crest: at s = 1 a full swing takes 4.4 s for small swings, 5.3 s at E = 0.30 J, and longer without limit as E approaches Vb.
See itSnap E onto the barrier height. Watch for: the ball crawling ever slower just right of the crest, while the time keeps running.
07

Two flat points, two kinds of balance

At x = ±1 m the slope is zero, so a ball at rest there feels no force and stays put. Both points are equilibria. The curvature V″ decides what a small nudge does:

  • Valley floor, V″ = +2s. Off the floor the force points back toward it, so a nudged ball oscillates. Small swings take 2π√(m/2s): 4.44 s at s = 1.
  • Crest, V″ = −2s. Off the crest the force points away from it, so any nudge grows. The same rate λ = √(2s/m) sets how fast it runs away.

The sim cannot place a ball at rest on the crest; section 06 shows the crest from the approach side.

See itDrop E to just above the valley floor. Watch for: the ball rocking in a small swing about x = +1 m, always pulled back.
08

Where it matters

  • A pendulum has the same structure. Below 2mgℓ it swings; above it, it goes over the top. At exactly 2mgℓ it creeps toward upside down and never gets there.
  • A chemical bond is a potential well. The H₂ molecule needs about 4.5 eV to break: with less, the two atoms vibrate; with more, they fly apart.
  • Escape speed. A body launched from Earth's surface at 11.2 km/s or more (ignoring air) has enough energy to climb out of Earth's gravity well and never return.
Go deeper: the pendulum's energy diagram
V(θ) = mgℓ(1 − cos θ). The crests at 2mgℓ are the upside-down position; the amber line is the pendulum's separatrix.
09

Summary

In one line. The height of E above the curve sets the speed; the height of E against the barrier sets the fate.

Key points

  • KE = E − V(x): speed peaks where V is lowest and is zero at the turning points.
  • The slope sets the acceleration, a = −V′(x)/m, not the speed.
  • Below Vb the ball is bound and swings forever; above Vb it escapes once.
  • At E = Vb exactly, the ball approaches the crest forever: the separatrix.

Common mix-ups

  • "Steeper means faster." Steep means the speed is changing fast. The speed is largest where the slope is zero, at the valley floor.
  • "Energy is conserved, so the speed is the same everywhere." E is constant, but its split between KE and V changes at every x.
  • "At E = Vb the ball reaches the top and stops there." It gets ever closer but never arrives.

Things to try on your own

  • Set s = 2, then raise E until the ball escapes. Check that the threshold matches Vb in Measurements (1.333 J).
  • Keep E fixed and move x₀ across the valley. Check that the turning points and top speed do not change.
